name: Russell's critique of 'the Dark Ages' as a Eurocentric label
plain_explanation: Russell argues that calling 600-1000 the 'Dark Ages' reflects an unwarranted concentration on Western Europe: during this same period China enjoyed the Tang dynasty's golden age of poetry, and Islamic civilization from Spain to India was brilliant and dominant in both power and culture. Western Europe's later global dominance was not foreordained and should not be read backward into this period.
precise_definition: Russell's explicit argument that the loss suffered by Christendom in this period 'was not lost to civilization, but quite the contrary,' and that most of the cultural content of Western civilization itself derives from the Eastern Mediterranean (Greeks and Jews), not from any innate Western superiority.
why_it_mattered: It reframes the entire period covered by Part II: what looks like darkness from a narrowly Western viewpoint was, globally, an era of other civilizations' brilliance, and Western dominance from the Renaissance onward is treated by Russell as historically contingent rather than natural or permanent.
historical_origin: Prompted by Russell's survey of the low point of Western Christendom around the year 1000, contrasted with contemporaneous Tang China and the Islamic Caliphate.
examples: The Tang dynasty as 'the greatest age of Chinese poetry'
'the brilliant civilization of Islam' flourishing 'from India to Spain'
competing_positions: The conventional Eurocentric narrative that treats the whole world as passing through a 'Dark Age' in this period
